title: Felix and the Ledger
premise: When the coffin of Harrowgate's revered founder, Edmund Voss, is exhumed for a cemetery relocation and found empty, concierge Tamsin Ishikawa is pulled in because the only witness to the original 1974 burial once stayed at his hotel. Tamsin realizes the killer is someone who has studied the town's sealed case files obsessively, feeding him clues through guest ledger entries he alone can read. As the statute of limitations on the original crime nears, Tamsin must decide whether loyalty to the family that gave him refuge matters more than the truth, ultimately exposing the killer: the founder's own great-granddaughter, who hid the body decades ago to protect her father's name.
about_author: Astrid Eastwick spent a decade working night desks at grand hotels across the English coast, collecting the small betrayals guests leave behind in registration books. She writes mysteries about people who see everything and are seen by no one.

chapters.title: The Empty Box
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Tamsin Ishikawa, watching from the hotel lobby as the exhumation crowd disperses in stunned silence. The coffin held stones and a 1974 newspaper. Tamsin's pride in being unnoticed curdles into dread when a detective asks him, by name, what he knows. Emotional beat: the invisible man becomes visible against his will.

chapters.title: Ledger Lines
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. He reviews the hotel's archived guest ledgers from 1974 and finds an entry signed 'E.V.' dated three days after Voss's supposed burial. Detective Sergeant Okafor dismisses it as coincidence. Tamsin notices the handwriting matches a current guest. Beat: the thrill of the hunt awakening a long-dormant confidence.

chapters.title: The Founder's Shadow
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. A portrait of the investigation's constraints: the statute expires in six weeks, the Voss family controls the archives, and the town council wants the exhumation quietly forgotten. Okafor privately doubts Tamsin's motives. Beat: institutional pressure tightening like a vise.

chapters.title: Guest 214
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. He identifies the ledger hand as Marguerite Voss-Lane, the founder's great-granddaughter, staying under her married name. She is charming, generous, and asks oddly precise questions about the hotel's history. Tamsin says nothing, telling himself it's discretion. Beat: the first compromise between truth and comfort.

chapters.title: What the Night Porter Saw
chapters.summary: POV of elderly former porter Cyril Bannerman, the sole living witness to the 1974 burial. He recalls a second, smaller coffin carried out through the service entrance before dawn. That night his cottage is ransacked. Beat: the past reaching forward with violence.

chapters.title: A Debt of Rooms
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Flashback woven into present: the Voss family paid for his mother's care when he was seventeen, binding him to them with gratitude. Now Marguerite offers him the archivist position he's always wanted. Beat: belonging offered as a leash.

chapters.title: Stones and Paper
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Forensics confirm the coffin stones came from the Voss estate quarry. Okafor confronts Tamsin about withholding the ledger entry; their fragile alliance cracks. Tamsin hands over a copy but keeps the original page. Beat: loyalty splitting down the middle.

chapters.title: The Second Coffin
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Following Cyril's account, he searches the hotel's sealed sub-basement and finds scratch marks and a rotted tarp — evidence something was stored there in 1974. Someone has been there recently; a fresh cigarette butt lies among the dust. Beat: the hunter realizing he is also hunted.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Tea
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, intimate and controlled. She reflects on her father's deathbed confession and her fifty-year guardianship of the family myth. She invites Tamsin to tea and quotes his own private observations back to him. Beat: power revealed — she has been reading him all along.

chapters.title: Cyril's Silence
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Cyril Bannerman is found dead, officially a fall down his stairs. The statute clock ticks louder. Okafor suspects Tamsin's inquiries flushed Cyril into the open. Beat: guilt and grief hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Archivist's Key
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. He accepts Marguerite's offer, gaining access to the family archive, and finds pages razored from the 1974 correspondence — cut by someone with archival training. He photographs everything, playing the grateful employee. Beat: deception as survival, self-loathing simmering.

chapters.title: Letters Never Sent
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Recovered letters show Edmund Voss planned to disinherit his son days before his death, and that the son had a motive and means. But the son died in 1989 — so who maintained the cover-up since? Beat: the mystery deepens beyond a single culprit.

chapters.title: Night Audit
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Working the overnight desk, he cross-references forty years of ledgers and finds the same distinctive marginalia appearing every few years — corrections, annotations, a curator's hand keeping the legend alive. The hand belongs to someone still employed by the hotel. Beat: the trap closing inward, toward home.

chapters.title: The Understudy
chapters.summary: POV of hotel manager Greta Solheim, Tamsin's mentor, who taught him to notice everything. Her chapter reveals her long, quiet devotion to the Voss legacy — and her awareness that Tamsin is digging. Beat: betrayal foreshadowed by tenderness.

chapters.title: Statute of Limitations
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Legal counsel warns that in eleven days the case dies forever. Okafor and Tamsin reconcile, pooling what each withheld. They agree the killer must be provoked into one final act. Beat: alliance rebuilt on shared guilt over Cyril.

chapters.title: Bait in the Ledger
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. He plants a fabricated ledger entry claiming a guest saw the 1974 transfer and kept photographs, then waits. At 3 a.m., the archive room light is on. Beat: cold fear and steely purpose as the trap springs.

chapters.title: Greta's Hands
chapters.summary: Confrontation in the archive. Greta, not Marguerite, moved the body in 1974 as a young maid protecting the son she loved; Marguerite has merely curated the lie since. Greta begs Tamsin to remember who gave him a life. Beat: the climax of loyalty versus truth, weaponized intimacy.

chapters.title: Where the Body Lies
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Greta leads them to the old wellhouse on the Voss estate. Beneath the floor: remains consistent with Edmund Voss, plus a locket that breaks the family story open — the son was not the heir everyone believed. Beat: grim vindication shadowed by sorrow.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Confession
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Rather than fight, she dictates a full statement, revealing she discovered the truth at nineteen and chose the myth over justice, editing the ledgers herself for decades. She asks Tamsin whether he would have chosen differently. Beat: the corrupting comfort of power acknowledged without excuse.

chapters.title: The Last Entry
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. He closes the case file and writes the final annotation in the ledger himself — the truth, unredacted — then resigns from the hotel. Greta is arrested; Marguerite awaits trial. Beat: grief, relief, and the cost of visibility fully felt.

chapters.title: Checkout
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, weeks later. The town turns on him as the man who broke Harrowgate's founding legend; old friends stop speaking. Packing his single suitcase, he finds an envelope from Okafor: a job offer consulting on cold cases. Beat: exile transformed into a door opening.

chapters.title: Felix and the Ledger
chapters.summary: Epilogue in Tamsin's first-person voice for the first time. In a new town, at a new desk, he registers a guest whose signature makes his breath catch — another hidden history waiting. He opens a fresh ledger and writes his own name on the first line. Beat: belonging redefined; the observer finally signs himself in.
